description: We are second year students at UBB, studying AI & computer science.
summary:
NASA's 24 combustion investigations sit in the public Physical Science Informatics (PSI) database. A crew facing a spacecraft fire needs two answers: will it spread, and what puts it out? The archive does not answer them directly: it holds hundreds of files per experiment, including videos whose outcomes are not in the PSI table.

We built burnrate, a website where a visitor picks a cabin's air (oxygen, pressure, airflow) and sees what NASA's flight tests say about it. Our open tracker follows the flame in NASA's BASS-II videos and turns each test into measurements: when the flame ignited, when it went out and how fast it spread. So far 18 of 22 B-series tests are measured. A suppression test bench on NASA's FLEX droplet tests shows, for each mix of oxygen and added gas, how hot a flame could get and which mixes were never flown. Every test opens its PSI source, and the site says what was never tested.

The next crews fly to the Moon and Mars, where cabin air and gravity differ from the tests that exist. burnrate shows engineers where the evidence is thin and makes NASA's open data usable for researchers and students.
details:
THE CHALLENGE

NASA asks for a dashboard that summarizes, ranks and interprets the PSI combustion experiments so that fire-safety insight is easier to reach. Fire in a spacecraft is a hard problem: the fire-safety pillars are prevention (which materials burn, and under what air), detection (will smoke be noticed) and suppression (what stops a flame). We built two analyses: Video to Data (how a flame spreads and when it goes out) and the Suppression test bench (what puts a flame out); detection is covered only through the catalog.

WHAT IT DOES

A catalog of all 24 PSI combustion investigations. Each has our plain-language summary (written with SI help, labelled as such), tags for fire-safety pillar, fuel phase and hardware, a page per investigation and a tests explorer that puts every test from the 22 experimental tables on one shared set of columns, each traced to its file and row.

A cabin air control (oxygen, pressure, airflow) that every page reads, and a ranking of the 24 investigations for that air, with the reason for each position written out. Marks under the oxygen and pressure sliders show where the 727 tests that state both ran, and one button moves the sliders to the nearest tested air and names that test.

A Video to Data page built on PSI-25 (BASS-II): for each measured test, the clip with the tracked flame edge drawn on it, the events (ignition, extinction, still burning at the end) and the spread rate in pixels per second with an interval and warning flags. Of the 18 measured tests, 6 show a steady spread with no warning flag; the others keep their flags in view. Checks: in test B1 the flame left the video 1.6 s after the fan began to slow, matching NASA's report ("within 2 s"); a blind SI grader matched NASA's published outcome in 10 of 11 fabric (T-series) tests, with 1 undecided and 0 contradictions (blind, against NASA's Table 7.1, labelled SI-made in the data); and the tracker against SI-made markings, checked by a team member, on 5 tests (mean difference 2.5 pixels per second, 26%, mostly from one test where the tracker followed only a bright burst; shown test by test on the Video to Data page, as not passing our own 25% limit). No independent hand measurement and no comparison with NASA's published spread rates exist yet (pixels against millimetres).

A Suppression test bench page built on PSI-69 (FLEX). It opens with what the flight tests show, counted from the FLEX table: with nitrogen only, the flame went out in 30 of 33 tests at 12 to 15% oxygen but in 2 of 24 at 30 to 34%; at 19 to 21% oxygen it went out in 32 of 41 tests with carbon dioxide added against 17 of 34 with nitrogen only. Below that, for 273 of the 274 FLEX tests it computes the hottest temperature the flame could reach and how fast heat spreads in that gas mix (a calculated, ideal value, not a measurement). It shows where the flown tests stop: none of the 173 tests with carbon dioxide or helium went above 25% oxygen, and all 24 tests at 30 to 34% oxygen used nitrogen only. Helium is flagged as the place where temperature alone does not explain the result. We check the calculation against NASA's own calculated (adiabatic) flame temperatures in PSI-10 (off by 2.5 K at the median over 147 flames). For a chosen mixture, the bench also shows a prediction of how much more carbon dioxide or how much less oxygen would make the flame burn out sooner. It is a model fitted to the FLEX tests, off by about 13 points of fuel burned on test days it never saw, and it is labelled as a prediction, not a result. Under "Never tested" it proposes the next experiment: 6 gas mixtures at 30 to 34% oxygen to fly together, picked to be far from every real test and from each other. They cut the largest gap in that region from 0.76 to 0.24 (a distance in slider widths, not a prediction of what a flame would do); the first 6 rows of a plain ranked list would leave 0.45.

An evidence panel: a value opens the same panel, which shows how the value was made (video measured, published, read from the PSI table, hand measured, calculated, or SI extracted), the PSI file and a link back to psi.nasa.gov.

A Compare page puts up to four investigations side by side, one row per field that PSI states for each of them (from the catalog's compare route).

A Limitations page gathers what the data cannot tell in one place: for the whole site, for each analysis and for each investigation, each line with its source.

Scenarios set real spacecraft fires against the data, as "what happened versus what burnrate would have shown". Artemis II (2026): the fire alarm 80,000 miles from home, against the 15 BASS-II flames (PSI-25) whose fan was turned down in orbit: 7 went out within 2.0 s, 7 had already gone, and one (B8) kept burning 6.2 s; and the Moon-base air, where 0 of 274 FLEX suppression tests (PSI-69) ran. Apollo 1 (1967): the fire on the Apollo 204 Review Board's own clock, and its cabin air (100% oxygen at 16.7 psi) checked against the range of the catalogued PSI tests: it sits outside, so the site would have flagged it as untested air. Apollo 13, Mir 1997 and a future Moon base get one sentence each. Thought experiments on published data, not claims about what could have been prevented.

Smoke detection is a filter of the Investigations list (4 investigations: SAME, SAME-R, DAFT and a ground study). There is no detection engine: we did not compute new detection numbers.

Ask burnrate, an assistant that answers questions in plain language. It can only use this site's own data service (catalog, tests and the two engines) through tools, and every citation it writes is checked against what those tools returned before it is shown; a citation the check cannot match is removed.

HOW IT WORKS

An offline pipeline reads the raw PSI files and writes three things: a catalog database, and, for each engine, a folder with the same three files (a description, one record per value per test, and the headline numbers and checks). One validator checks the folders. A single read-only backend (FastAPI) serves them and the website (Next.js) shows them.

WHAT IS NEW COMPARED WITH THE PSI SITE

PSI lets you search investigations and download files. We add one table across all tests, a view by cabin air instead of by investigation, and numbers measured from the BASS-II videos, which PSI holds only as video. Every page shows its checks, including the ones that have not passed or not run yet.

WHAT THE DATA CANNOT TELL

No PSI test was run in Moon or Mars gravity. Most flight tests are small and use one material, one size and one fuel at a time; the table for BASS-II has no spread-rate or outcome column, so those numbers come from the videos. A dim flame can vanish from video before it is out, and without a scale in the frame the spread rates cannot be given in millimetres per second. The Suppression test bench temperatures are calculated for ideal burning, not measured, and the coldest mix that still burned in a flight test is the edge of what was tested, not a measured extinction limit. Near-identical FLEX tests already differ by about 7 points in share of fuel burned, so no model can be more precise than that. Droplet and gas-flame experiments say little about a cabin fire. The ranking shows where the evidence is, not which material is safe, and nothing here is a safety certification.

BENEFITS

Crew-safety engineers and mission designers see which tests cover a cabin and which do not. Researchers get a cleaned, traceable table and video-derived numbers. Students and the public get plain-language summaries of what NASA tested and why.

WHO WE ASKED, AND WHAT WE CHANGED

On 14 November we wrote to about 110 combustion and fire-safety researchers and engineers, mostly authors of the NASA papers behind the PSI investigations (some twice, by LinkedIn after an email bounced). 15 replied in person by 15 November. Most said the experiments were outside their own work and pointed us to the NASA investigators. Those who answered the science agreed on one point: a calculated, ideal flame temperature does not by itself decide whether a flame goes out, and helium behaves differently because it carries heat differently. A researcher who worked on the FLEX droplet tests said he would expect our calculated FLEX temperatures to be correct. A reduced-gravity flammability researcher added that a standard flammability test ranks materials only at the sample size it tests, so its ranking is not universal, one more reason the site shows conditions next to every result. The Space Apps Navigator reviewed our wording in the public discussion. What changed: temperatures on the Suppression test bench are presented as calculated, not measured; helium is flagged as the case where temperature alone fails; the smoke detector claim we first sent out is not made anywhere in the product; a Limitations page gathers what the data cannot tell; and the test bench plots how every FLEX test ended against oxygen and added gas, as one researcher asked. Nobody named here has endorsed the project.

WHO PAYS

Nobody pays for the NASA data, which is public and free. Two groups have a reason and a budget to pay for the work on top of it. Commercial space-station builders such as Vast and Axiom have materials and safety teams that must show their materials are fit for crewed stations, so they could use a citable evidence summary per material and hazard: the PSI tests, their conditions and what was never tested. Fire test laboratories read flame positions from test videos by eye today, so they could run our video-to-data engine on their own videos, checked against their own hand readings. We make no revenue or savings claims, and none of these organizations has endorsed or used this.

WHAT WE HOPE TO ACHIEVE

To show that the archive can be used as a decision tool, and to give back to it: a list of PSI data pitfalls we hit, and requests for the next experiment.

TOOLS

Python (data pipeline), FastAPI (backend), Next.js (website), Modal for one training experiment, GitHub for source and an automated integrity check on every change. The full list is in the references field. SI assistance (Claude Code) is described in the next field.

SCREENSHOTS

Real screenshots of the live site (https://burnrate-psi-rosy.vercel.app), uploaded with this field: the overview, the investigations list, the PSI-25 page, the tests explorer, Video to Data on test B1, the Suppression test bench (what works, try a mixture), Compare, Limitations and Ask burnrate. Every data figure in this text appears in a module's findings.json or in the catalog database; the historical figures in the two scenarios come from the sources listed in the references field.
